content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a neural architecture search (NAS) formulation for object detection that aims to improve generalization when there is a mismatch between the test and training distributions
(the Out-of-Distribution setting). The method assumes that context-related class labels are available during training.
The key insight is to add a context classification head alongside the detection head and encourage dis-entanglement of the factors of variation between the two heads via a feature
orthogonality loss term.

Experiments show state-of-the-art results in the IID setting (on Pascal VOC 2007 and MS-COCO) and significantly better generalization in the OOD setting (on BDD100K) compared to alternatives that do not leverage contextual information.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* This work targets a relevant and less explored problem, that of Neural Architecture Search for object detection.
* To my knowledge, this is the first work to give theoretical guarantees for convergence in an OOD scenario.
* The type of contextual information used in the experiments (time of day, weather) is readily available on contemporary
vehicle fleets. Using it to enhance generalization is a sensible and cost-effective approach.

Weaknesses:

* This work does not introduce any new algorithms or techniques. Original papers (correctly cited by the authors):
  * ISTA-NAS (Yang et al., 2020)
  * FPN (Lin et al., 2017)
  * feature orthogonalization (Bai et al, 2020)

* Evaluation methodology raises some concerns:

  * Model sizes are not comparable. While there is indeed a Swin-B variant that is comparable to NAS-DO in Table 1 and
  Table 2 (145M vs. 153M & 143M), the other variants have much smaller parameter counts (e.g. NAS-FCOS 57M).
  * The accuracy reported for NAS-FCOS is widely different from result the original paper (Wang et. al, CVPR, 2021). 
  On MS-COCO, at the same number of parameters as in this work (cca. 57M), they report 43.0 AP (while this work reports
  1.8AP). Where does this huge difference come from?
  * Neural Architecture Search was re-run for each dataset in the IID case. The fact that a single model size is given
  in Table 1 for other methods suggests this was not done for NAS-based baselines. The authors should clarify the
  experimental setup.
  * Comparing to Swin-B (19.4 improvement) in Table 2 is not fair, as Swin-B does not have access to contextual labels.
  A fair comparison based on the numbers the authors provide would be NAS-DO with $\lambda_{ctx}=0$ against Swin-B,
  which would lead to $16.9$ / $12.1$ relative improvement on the weather condition and $1.8$ and -$7.0$ relative
  improvement on the time of day condition ($text{AP}_L$ and $text{AR}_L$).
  * Unlike on Pascal VOC and MS-COCO, average precision/recall is reported for objects with area greater than $96^{2}$.
  Why is this?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: * Clarity: * It is not immediately clear when reading the paper which methods use contextual information during training and which do not (especially as it would be easy to add a contextual classification head to most of the baselines). The confusion is further reinforced as the authors compare to Swin-B when giving their final improvement, showing a $19.4$, which suggests comparison given equal training information. I think the training information available to each method should be clear when reading the table (separate column or row highlighting), or, alternatively, results that use contextual information should be presented in a separate table. * It should be clearly stated how baselines were trained (e.g. explaining why different results with respect to original Swin-B accuracies were obtained and clarifying whether NAS was re-run for baseline methods on each problem). * On page 6, Theorem 3.4, I guess "Theorem 3.1" refers to "Assumption 3.1", "Theorem 3.2" refers to "Assumption 3.2", and "Theorem 3.3" refers to "Constraint 3.3". * In table 2, $\lambda_\text{ctx}$ is part of the BACKBONE column, but is unrelated to the backbone architecture (or architecture space, see "NAS SPACE" in Table 1). * It is never mentioned why the authors report average precision/recall for large objects only in Table 2. * Novelty: * The work is not novel with respect to introducing new techniques and algorithms (see weaknesses). Still, this is, up to my knowledge, the first time contextual information is used within a NAS framework for object detection. Also, the theoretical guarantees for convergence in an OOD scenario seem novel. * Quality: * I have concerns regarding the overall evaluation methodology: some comparisons are not fair (different model sizes NAS not re-run for baselines on each dataset) and it is not clear why the accuracy of the NAS-FCOS baseline is so low and different than reported in the original work. * Reproducibility: * While sufficient information for reproducing the method is provided, this does not seem to hold for reproducing baselines. * The authors do not mention any plans to provide public code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Leveraging contextual information to improve model generalization via feature dis-entanglement makes sense and is
easily applicable in practice. My main concern with this work is the evaluation protocol, as detailed in the review.
In particular, I think the authors should compare against methods with similar model sizes (they currently only do this
for Swin-B), should use their context free variant to report improvements against baselines in the OOD setting, and
should re-run architecture search for each NAS baseline against each dataset to let it adapt to the problem difficulty
(like they do with their method). The above does not necessarily imply running baselines with larger model sizes. It
should be at least as easy to constrain NAS-DO to a similar model size for each baseline, and turn on/off the contextual
information source/feature orthogonalization (for the OOD scenario). In the absence of a fair comparison on equal terms
with the baselines, it hard to judge whether the proposed NAS method is actually superior in both the IID and OOD
scenarios. I encourage the authors to clarify in their rebuttal the various unclear points (it may well be that I
misunderstood their experimental protocol).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of object detection with Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalizable neural architecture search. The main contribution is the split of the network to find and separate category-related to context-related features. This is achieved by using a neural network which architecture is optimized by neural architecture search (NAS) and splits to separate categories from context similar to a multitask network. To assure the complementarity of category identification vs context identification, orthogonality is imposed by minimizing the Frobenius norm of the weight matrices. Validation is done on MS COCO and BDD100K-weather and BDD100K-time-of-day.  Average precision and average recall for objects with area >96^2 is used to show and validate the final  results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths are as follows:
1. The NAS architexture chosen to address the problem is a solid and straighforward technique.
2. The idea of splitting category vs context objects is interesting.
3. The mathematical definition of the complementarity of the category vs context objects identification is straighforward.
4. Validation covers various public datasets, backbones, hyperparameters, with promising results  in most of the cases.

The weaknesses are:
1. The separation of context vs categories of interest is done manually, the network learns to differentiate both sets from the training data. Is the annotater who should decide what is context and what ar ethe categories of interest. It would be much more challenging that the network is capable to separate categories of interest vs. context in an unsupervised manner in the same way as for humans  in the case of "a car driving at night" they discover but are not trained that the night is part of the context.
2. The paper is about OOD but in fact validation is not following the standard procedure of validating an OOD technique where the network is trained on one domain and is applied to data from another domain.
3. Moreover, if the technique is really for OOD detection, it is recommended to follow the standard datasets for OOD like SVHN, LSUN, Places365, Clinc-Full, Clinc-Small, Cifar-100, OpenImages, CUB, Texture, etc.
4. It is difficult to compare to the state of the art since different measures are used. In OOD  detection the standard measures to validate the results are: FBR95, AUROC, AUPR. In the paper the measures to validate the results are the average precision and average recall.
5. There is no state of the art comparison.

Minor details:
1. Define the dimensions of W_{cls} and W_{ctx}.
2. In (4) the minimization is on L_{val}. In Algorithm 1, the minimization of parameters s is on L_{train}. Is this correct?
3. In Table 3 only a few parameters are studied for number of layers, steps and sparseness. It is not clear that they are the optimal ones.
4. Ablation study mixes study on the architecture, hyperparameters and the model performance.
5. Annotate or at least better explain where the parameters (A, z, s, w) fit the architecture in Fig.3.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well structured. The methodology is properly introduced and the mathematical formulation is technically sound although it is highly recommended to better explain where the different hyperparameters fit the main pipeline in Fig.3.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is introducing a novel model based on NAS that shows good performance due to the novel split of context vs category identification modules. Results are very encouraging. Still the paper needs several improvements as mentioned in the weakness part that need to be addressed before publishing. Moreover, it doesn't really seem to focus on OOD detection.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a neural architecture search (NAS) framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on object detection task. Concretely, the authors state that the spurious correlations of category-related features and context-related features limit the OOD performance, and therefore propose to search an optimal backbone architecture to disentangle category-related features and the context-related features. Numerical results on Pascal VOC, MS COCO, and BDD100K datasets are provided to validate the efficacy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. This paper proposes a feature orthogonalization method to explicitly disentangle the features into category features and context features, which seems effective in OOD task according to the theoretical analysis and empirical results in the paper.

2. The experimental results show that, the proposed NAS-DO model significantly outperforms previous models, especially on BDD100K dataset of OOD task.

Weaknesses:

1. I didn't get the necessity of combining NAS and feature orthogonalization. These two modules looks independent for me. Why must we use NAS-searched backbone for feature orthogonalization? Do the traditional backbones fail to work well with the feature orthogonalization? The paper should have an experiment on it.

2. The idea that adopting NAS in OOD is not novel, which has been introduced by NAS-OoD. Besides, the improvements of the newly-introduced feature orthogonalization module seems small according to the ablation study in Figure 4.

3. Some experimental results are not convincing for me to sufficient validate the effectiveness of the method. See questions for details.

Questions:
1. The indicator function in Equation (8) is non-differentiable, how to minimize it?
2. Why the authors sample 10K images from COCO train set instead of using the complete train set?
3. Why the authors report AP_L instead of the original AP metric in BDD100K? Is it a carefully-selected metric?
4. According to the visualizations in Figure 8, architectures obtrained on different datasets vary a lot. Can the authors show the transferabilities of the searched backbones among these datasets?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and ideas in this paper are easy to follow. The novelty seems limited for me. Some important details to reproduce the results are lacking in the paper, but code was provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the paper is below the acceptance threshold. My major concerns of this paper are the novelty of this work and the sufficiency of experiments.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
